name: BYTE-05
title: Unified Memory Is Not Free
subtitle: 128 GB looks great until you measure it

scenes.head: 128 GB unified vs 24 GB discrete
scenes.vo: Okay, so a machine with one hundred and twenty-eight gigabytes of unified memory will hold any model you can throw at it. That part is true. So why does it feel slower than a gaming card with a fifth of the memory? Because bandwidth is not capacity, and the benchmark measured both machines on the same model.

scenes.head: m5 max · 128 gb unified
scenes.vo: On an M5 Max with one hundred and twenty-eight gigabytes, Qwen three point eight generates thirty-one point four tokens a second at four K. At sixteen K it is twenty-three point six. At thirty-two K, twenty-one point six. At sixty-four K, eighteen point two. That is a real machine doing real work, and it is slower than a three thousand ninety at every single row.

scenes.head: gb10 · the small box
scenes.vo: The GB10 box is the same story with a smaller number. Twelve point two tokens a second at four K. Eleven point nine at eight K. Ten point eight at thirty-two K. Nine point seven at sixty-four K. Eight at one twenty-eight K. And five point nine four at two hundred fifty-six K. It will hold the context. It will not move quickly through it.

scenes.head: same model, three machines
scenes.vo: Put them in one table. At four K, the three thousand ninety does forty-five, the M5 Max does thirty-one, the GB10 does twelve. At sixty-four K, thirty-four, eighteen, and eight. The memory ceiling is the opposite order. The machine with the most memory is the slowest, by a factor of four.

scenes.head: what unified memory is for
scenes.vo: Two caveats, and they matter. Unified memory is genuinely better when the model does not fit anywhere else, and it is quieter and cheaper to run than four cards. And this measures a dense thirty billion parameter model. A machine with one hundred and twenty-eight gigabytes can hold something no consumer card can, and that is worth something real.
items: Wins when the model fits nowhere else

scenes.head: the honest summary
scenes.vo: So the summary is not that unified memory is bad. It is that you should buy it for the model that does not fit, not for the speed. If your model fits on a twenty-four gigabyte card, the discrete card wins on tokens per second, on prefill, and on price. If it does not fit, the unified machine is the only door.

scenes.head: m5 max prefill
scenes.vo: Prefill on the M5 Max tells the same story. Eight hundred and thirty-four tokens a second at a short prompt, falling to four hundred and twenty-four at longer context. On the three thousand ninety, Glimmer does fourteen hundred and seventy-six and still holds five hundred and eighty-four at two hundred fifty-six K. The unified machine is not slow because it is badly built. It is slow because it is feeding a very wide model from memory that is not a graphics card.

scenes.head: gb10 prefill
scenes.vo: The GB10 is lower again. Eight hundred and twelve tokens a second at four K, falling to two hundred and twenty-eight at two hundred fifty-six K. That is a machine that will hold the context and then take minutes to read it. For an agent that re-reads a large codebase on every step, that is the difference between usable and unusable.

cues.2: two hundred and twenty-eight at two hundred

scenes.head: what unified memory is genuinely for
scenes.vo: So be fair to it. Unified memory is the only way to hold a model that does not fit on any consumer card, and it does that at a fraction of the power and noise of a four card rig. It is also the only option on a laptop, where a discrete card with that much memory does not exist. The mistake is buying it for speed, because speed is the one thing it does not sell.

scenes.head: the full comparison
scenes.vo: Here is everything in one place. At four K, the three thousand ninety does forty-five point three, the M5 Max does thirty-one point four, the GB10 does twelve point two, and the two-card setup does twenty-two point four seven. At sixty-four K it is thirty-four, eighteen, eight, and eighteen point five. Sort by memory and you get one order. Sort by speed and you get the exact opposite.

scenes.head: the honest limits of this test
scenes.vo: Two limits. These are dense models, and a mixture of experts model activates a fraction of its parameters per token, so the bandwidth penalty shrinks and unified memory looks much better. And this is one benchmark on one software build. Treat the ratio as a shape, not a law, and measure your own model before you spend four figures on a machine.
items: Dense models only: MoE behaves differently
One build, one benchmark: shape, not law

scenes.head: a 5090 for scale
scenes.vo: For scale, a five-oh-ninety does eighty-three point two tokens a second on Glimmer at four K, and sixty-eight point nine eight at two hundred fifty-six K. That is not a subtle difference from twelve point seven on the GB10. It is roughly six and a half times faster, on a card that also costs less than the small box. Unified memory is a capacity purchase, and the numbers make that unavoidable.

scenes.head: the laptop case is different
scenes.vo: But the laptop case is genuinely different, and it deserves saying. A laptop with unified memory is the only way to run a large model on battery, quietly, with no external power supply. A three thousand ninety in a laptop does not exist. So if portability is the requirement, unified memory is not a compromise, it is the category. You are not choosing between fast and slow, you are choosing between possible and impossible.

scenes.head: what to measure before buying
scenes.vo: Before you buy either, measure two things. Tokens per second at the context you actually use, and time to first token at the prompt length you actually paste. Those two numbers describe the entire experience. Everything else on a spec sheet, including the memory figure that started this video, is a proxy that can mislead you in either direction.
items: Tokens per second at your context
Time to first token at your prompt length

scenes.head: when unified actually wins
scenes.vo: Unified memory wins in three specific situations. The model does not fit on any consumer card. You need it to run on a laptop or on battery. Or you need it quiet, because a workstation that sounds like a hairdryer is not usable in a room with other people. None of those are speed arguments, and all of them are legitimate. Buy it for those reasons and you will be happy.

scenes.head: the number that decides it
scenes.vo: If you take one number from this video, take the ratio. Forty-five point three tokens a second on a discrete card against twelve point seven six on the small unified box, for the same model at the same context. That is three and a half times. If that gap does not matter to your workload, buy the quiet machine. If it does, buy the card, and stop paying for memory you are not using.

scenes.head: the one sentence version
scenes.vo: One sentence. Unified memory buys you capacity and silence, and it charges you in tokens per second, roughly three and a half times the price of a discrete card at four K and even more at long context. Buy it when the model does not fit anywhere else, or when it has to live on a laptop. Do not buy it expecting speed, because the entire design is a trade away from speed.

scenes.head: close
scenes.vo: So stop reading the memory number first. Read the bandwidth, then the measured tokens per second, then the capacity. In that order the machine chooses itself, and you stop paying for gigabytes you will never fill.
